entries.narration: Every number this pipeline will publish starts in one place: TradeBook, the trade finance desk's own database. On Ana's laptop it is a local PostgreSQL copy, filled by the course's data generator, and everything in this frame runs locally. The schema in the editor has three tables, and the side pane draws them. Counterparty holds the desk's clients, each a legal entity; notice there is no group here, because TradeBook does not know which companies belong together. L C deals holds one row per letter of credit, and only its current version: when an L C is amended, its row is overwritten. L C amendments keeps every version an L C has ever had. Two columns in L C deals carry the whole pipeline, and they are highlighted. Source version counts an L C's revisions, one, two, three. Updated at records when the row last changed, and it is indexed, because every night we will ask for the rows that changed since the night before. The terminal creates the tables, loads the seed, and counts the L Cs by status: four hundred in all, most of them already finished, expired, closed or cancelled, and the rest still open. Next, one letter of credit's whole life.

To measure exposure, the pipeline needs one rule: which letters of credit still count. The side pane follows one L C through its life, read from L C amendments by a saved query. Version one: it is issued, in June, for six hundred and forty seven thousand dollars. Version two: it is advised to the exporter and becomes active. Version three: it is amended, and the amount drops to four hundred and seventy six thousand. Version four: it is closed, and from that moment the bank's promise is over. That is the rule in the editor, in open dot s q l. An L C that is issued, active or amended is open, and its amount is exposure: money the bank has promised to pay. An L C that is expired, closed or cancelled carries no exposure at all, though it stays in the data. Notice the last line, group by currency. The terminal shows why. There are forty open L Cs in euros and ninety in dollars, and their totals are printed side by side, never added together, because a sum of dollars and euros is not a number anyone can use. The pipeline will keep that rule all the way to Gold. Next, Azure, and the first sign in.

Now Azure. Ana has signed in with a z login, and from here on every frame marked recorded on Azure was run once on a real subscription, with its identifiers replaced before anything was saved. The map is the whole pipeline we will build, and right now every part of it is grey: nothing exists yet. The terminal confirms it. The account shows the subscription, sub tradefin dev, and who is signed in. U K South is the region the pipeline will live in. The search for anything named tradefin returns nothing at all. And the storage provider is registered, so the subscription is allowed to create storage accounts. Before creating anything, two conventions, in the side pane. Every name says what it is, which app it belongs to, and which environment: r g for a resource group, s t for a storage account, k v for a key vault, a d f for Data Factory, then tradefin, then dev. A storage account's name cannot hold hyphens, so it runs together. And every resource carries three tags, each answering a question someone will ask one day: which app is this for, which environment, so can I delete it, and who owns it, so who do I call. Next, the first resource, written as code.

The pipeline's infrastructure is written as code, with Terraform, and this is the first file. Main dot t f names the provider, azure r m, pinned to one exact version, and declares two resources: the resource group, with its three tags, and the storage account that will become the lake, with account keys switched off from the start. Nothing in the file says how to create them, only what should exist. The terminal runs it. Init downloads the pinned provider. Apply compares the file with what exists, finds nothing, and plans two additions; then it creates them, and the run ends with two resources added. The side pane shows the path a block of code takes. Terraform reads main dot t f; the provider turns each block into calls to Azure Resource Manager, the one A P I behind the portal, the C L I and every other tool; and Resource Manager creates the account in U K South. State list names what Terraform now manages: the resource group and the storage account. Look at the last line, the folder listing. Terraform has written a file called terraform dot t f state, on Ana's laptop, and it is how Terraform knows what it created. Next, why that file cannot stay there.

Terraform's state is its memory: which real resource each block of code became. On a laptop it is one person's, and it can be lost. So it moves into Azure. The new file, backend dot t f, points Terraform at a container called t f state, in a storage account of its own, with one blob per environment, read with Ana's identity rather than a key. That account has to exist before Terraform can use it, so a small script, bootstrap dot s h, creates it with the C L I: the only thing in this course the C L I creates. The terminal runs it, then init with migrate state, which copies the local state into the blob; the listing shows dev dot t f state. The side pane draws what Terraform compares on every plan: the code, the state, and Azure itself. The state also needs a lock, so two people never apply at once, and the lock is the blob's lease. To see it, the session takes the lease by hand. The next plan fails at once: error acquiring the state lock, the state blob is already locked. The lease is broken, and the same plan runs, and finds no changes. Next, the code is reshaped for more than one environment.

The first file named everything by hand: dev appeared in every name. Production will need the same resources with different names, so the code is reshaped, and this frame is compiled: it runs offline, and deploys nothing. Main dot t f now takes one variable, e n v, and builds every name from it: r g tradefin, then the environment. The tags are written once, in locals, and passed on. The storage account moves into a module of its own, modules slash storage, which takes four inputs: a name, a resource group, a location and tags. The dev values live in a small file, envs slash dev dot t f vars, with one line: env equals dev. The two blocks at the bottom matter more than they look. The resources now have new addresses in the code, and without being told, Terraform would destroy the old ones and create new ones. Moved blocks tell it that these are the same resources under new names. The terminal checks the work without touching Azure: format reports the files are formatted, init with no backend fetches the provider, and validate finds the configuration valid. The listing shows the new tree, and the side pane draws it: the variables file, the root module, the storage module. Next, applying it, and what plan does to change made outside the code.

The reshaped code meets Azure, recorded once on the subscription. The first apply reads the moved blocks: the resource group and the storage account have moved to new addresses, and the plan adds nothing, changes nothing and destroys nothing. Then someone changes Azure without touching the code: an a z tag update sets the resource group's owner tag to ops. This is drift, and the next plan finds it: it shows the owner tag going from ops back to trade risk, one resource to change. Apply puts it back, and reading the tag again shows trade risk. The code wins, every time it is applied. The side pane lists the three cases plan can meet. A resource in the code and in the state, changed in Azure, is drift, and plan changes it back: that is what we just saw. A resource in the state but deleted from the code is something Terraform made and is now told to forget, and plan destroys it. And a resource made by hand in Azure, in neither the code nor the state, is invisible to Terraform altogether: plan says nothing, which is why this course makes every resource with code. Next, a budget, so the subscription warns before it spends.

Last in this course, a budget, recorded on Azure. Two resources are added to main dot t f. The first is an action group, a g trade risk: a list of who to tell when something happens, here one email address for the risk team's engineers. The second is a monthly budget on the resource group. Its notification is the highlighted part: when the forecast for the month passes eighty percent of the budget, tell the action group. Forecast, not actual: the forecast is the month's spending so far, projected to the month's end, so the warning comes early enough to act on, not after the money is gone. The terminal applies both, the action group and the budget, and the budget list shows it exists. The side pane draws the chain: the budget, the forecast crossing eighty percent, the action group, and an email. Notice what is missing. A budget warns; it never stops anything. Turning resources off is a decision for a person, or for automation someone has written on purpose, and this course tears its resources down after recording each part, so that nothing waits on the subscription between recordings. Next, before the pipeline holds anything, who is allowed to touch it.

Before the pipeline touches any data, it needs to be someone. In Azure, everything that acts has an identity, and the side pane lists the three kinds. A user is a person, like Ana, with a password and a second factor, hers alone. A service principal is an identity for an application: this very session runs as one, as the last line of the terminal shows, and somewhere a secret or a certificate proves it is who it says. And a managed identity is an identity for code that runs inside Azure, with one difference that matters: nobody stores its secret, because Azure holds the credential and hands out tokens itself. The Terraform block in the editor creates one for the pipeline: i d tradefin pipeline, a user assigned managed identity, which means it is a resource of its own, and can be given to Data Factory when Course seven builds it. The apply adds it, and the listing shows its name and its principal I D, the identifier that roles will be granted to. At the bottom of the side pane is how it will be used. Data Factory, wearing this identity, asks Entra I D for a token at run time; the token is short lived; and Key Vault or the lake checks the token, then checks the role. No password appears anywhere in that chain. Next, what a role is, and where it applies.

This detour draws how Azure decides what anyone may do, and every value in it was recorded on the subscription. A role assignment has exactly three parts, listed at the bottom right. Who: a principal, here the pipeline's identity. What: a role, which is a named list of allowed actions; Reader allows looking at anything and changing nothing. And where: a scope. The Terraform block grants Reader on the resource group. The left side is the scope hierarchy, nested the way Azure nests it. The outer box is the subscription. Two assignments live there, both Owner: the subscription's owner, and the service principal recording this course. Inside it is the resource group, which holds one assignment of its own, the new Reader. The terminal asks each scope in turn. At the subscription: Owner, Owner. At the resource group: only Reader. Then the same group, with inherited assignments included: Owner, Owner and Reader. That last list is the rule to remember. A role granted at a scope applies to everything beneath it, so an Owner of the subscription is an Owner of every resource group and every resource in it, without a single assignment at those levels. Granting high in the tree is easy, and it is how access quietly grows too wide. Next, a surprise: what Owner cannot do.

The session's identity is Owner of the whole subscription. Surely it can read the lake. The terminal tries, recorded on Azure. First it lists the storage account's containers, and that works: an empty list, because none exist yet. Then it lists the blobs in a container, and Azure refuses: you do not have the required permissions, and it names the roles that would grant them, every one a data role. The side pane explains why. Azure has two planes. The control plane manages resources: the account, its settings, its containers, and that is what Owner and Contributor grant. The data plane is the contents: the blobs inside, the secrets inside a vault. Owner grants nothing there, so a person who can delete the account still cannot read what is in it, which is exactly what a bank wants. The fix is in the editor. The storage module grants Storage Blob Data Contributor to whoever applies it, on this one account and nowhere else. The root module does the same for Key Vault's data plane, Key Vault Secrets Officer, on this resource group, ready for the next section. The apply adds both. One more thing the side pane notes: a new role takes a minute or two to reach the data plane, so the proof comes at the start of the next section. Next, a vault for the one password the pipeline needs.

The pipeline needs exactly one secret: the password Data Factory will use to read TradeBook. It belongs in a vault, and this section builds one, recorded on Azure. First, the proof the last section promised. Listing the blobs again no longer says permission denied; it says the container does not exist, which means the identity is now allowed to look. The data role has arrived. The editor shows the new Key Vault module. Two lines matter. R B A C authorization is on, so the same role assignments as everywhere else decide who may read a secret, instead of the vault's older access policies. And purge protection is off, because this course deletes its vault after every recording, and a protected vault's name could not be used again for days. The apply creates the vault. Then the password. Open S S L makes twenty four random bytes, straight into a shell variable; a z keyvault secret set stores them as tradebook password; and the variable is unset. The value was never printed, never written to a file, and never passed through Terraform, so it is not in the state either. The listing shows the secret's name, and only its name. The side pane draws the vault, the secret, and its versions: setting it again makes version two, and the name stays the same. Next, who may read it.

The password is in the vault. Now the pipeline must be allowed to read it, and nothing else. The Terraform block in the editor grants one role, Key Vault Secrets User, to the pipeline's managed identity, on this one vault. Secrets User can read a secret's value; it cannot create, change or delete one. The apply adds the assignment, recorded on Azure. The terminal then asks the vault who holds what, inherited assignments included, and the table in the side pane is that answer. The subscription's two Owners inherit down to the vault, the pipeline identity's Reader comes from the resource group, Ana's Secrets Officer lets her manage the secret, and the new line, Secrets User, belongs to the pipeline. The chain at the top is how the password will travel when Data Factory runs. The managed identity, which has no secret of its own, asks Entra I D for a token; the token lasts minutes and is good only for the vault; the vault checks the role and returns the password. At no point does anyone type it, store it in code, or see it. The last command proves the project's side of that promise: a search through every file for a password being assigned finds nothing at all. Next, the whole set of roles, checked against what each one needs.

With a few roles granted, it is worth stepping back and looking at all of them at once, which is how an auditor would. The terminal lists every role assignment on a scope with tradefin in its name, recorded on Azure, with each scope cut to its last part, and the table in the side pane is that list. Each row should answer three questions, written underneath. Is this the narrowest role that does the job? The pipeline identity reads, so it has Reader and Secrets User, never Contributor. Is this the narrowest scope? The data roles sit on one storage account and one vault, not on the subscription; the second Storage Blob Data Contributor is on the Terraform state's own account, where Ana must read and write state. And is the holder the right kind of principal? The pipeline acts as itself, never as a person. Least privilege is not a setting you switch on; it is this list, reviewed whenever it changes. The editor shows the other half of this section's apply: two policy assignments, written in a new file, policy dot t f. One allows only U K regions, and the other requires an owner tag on every resource. The apply adds both, and the last listing shows their names. Next, what they do to someone who ignores them.

Roles decide who may act. Policy decides what any action may create, whoever does it and with whatever tool, and this section tests it, recorded on Azure. The editor shows policy dot t f. Each rule starts as a definition, here two of Azure's built in ones, found by their names: allowed locations, and require a tag on resources. A definition does nothing until it is assigned to a scope with its parameters, and the two assignments put them on the resource group: the U K regions only, and a tag called owner. The side pane draws that chain: a definition, an assignment, and then a deny, which happens before anything is created. The terminal plays the person who skips the rules. The first attempt creates a storage account by hand in West Europe, and Azure refuses it: request disallowed by policy, naming the location rule. The second tries U K South, but with no tags, and is refused again, this time naming the tag rule. Neither command reached the point of creating anything, and the final listing shows the resource group still holds exactly one storage account, the lake. A role would have allowed both commands; the policy stopped them. Next course, the lake itself, and a batch the pipeline can trust.

The storage account has existed since Course three, on the map in the middle of the resource group, ringed. Now it has to become a lake, recorded once on Azure. The Terraform module on the right gains one highlighted line: the hierarchical namespace is switched on, which is what makes an account A D L S Gen two rather than a plain blob store. Account keys stay off, as they have been from the start. The plan shows something one line of code would not suggest: the storage account must be replaced. The hierarchical namespace is chosen when an account is created, and cannot be switched on for an account that already exists, so Terraform destroys the old account and creates a new one with the same name; the data role that sat on the old account goes with it, and is granted again. That is safe today only because the account is still empty, which is the reason to decide this early. The apply destroys two resources and adds two. The queries underneath read the new account back: the hierarchical namespace is true, and the account answers on two addresses, the blob endpoint and the D F S endpoint, the Data Lake A P I. The table shows what the switch changes. Without it, a folder is only part of each file's name, and renaming one means copying every file under it. With it, a folder is a real directory, and a rename is one operation. Next, the zones inside it.

Inside the account, the lake is divided into zones, and each zone is a container, which A D L S calls a file system. On the map, all five now have colour inside the storage account. The Terraform is one resource block with a for each over five names, so the list of zones lives in exactly one place. Like the account, the containers are made through the control plane, the management A P I. Terraform plans five additions and applies them. Then the session switches to the data plane, signed in as the same identity, with no key: the listing returns the five zones. Next, one command creates a directory inside landing, lc deals, then batch I D equals forty two, and the listing beneath shows two directories, the parent and the child, made in one call. On a flat namespace there would be nothing to list until a file existed. The table on the right says what each zone will hold, and when the course fills it. Landing receives TradeBook's batches exactly as delivered. Bronze keeps every version received. Silver keeps one current row per letter of credit. Gold holds the answer, exposure by group and currency. And reference holds the risk team's mapping and limits. Each zone has one job, so each can have its own access rules and its own retention. Next, a batch lands in landing.

The pipeline's first real job is to land TradeBook's letters of credit in the lake, and land them in a way we can trust later. On Ana's laptop the lake is Azurite, Azure Storage's emulator, and the label at the top of the side pane says so. Extract dot p y reads every L C that TradeBook held up to the window's end, two o'clock on the thirty first of October, and writes them as one C S V file. The path is the idea: the landing container, then lc deals, then a folder named batch I D equals forty one. Each night's copy gets a folder of its own, and the upload refuses to overwrite. The terminal shows both sides of that rule. The first run writes four hundred rows. The same command again, a retry or a careless double click, is refused, because the file already exists. A delivery, once written, never changes under the people reading it. The table in the side pane shows why two numbers are needed. Source version is TradeBook's count of one L C's revisions. The batch I D names the delivery that carried a row. This letter of credit arrives at version one, for two million dollars, in batch forty one; tomorrow its amendment, version two, arrives in batch forty two. Bronze will keep both. Next, we stop copying everything, and copy only what changed.

Batch forty one was a full load. Since then, the desk has worked through the whole of the thirty first of October, issuing, amending and closing letters of credit, and copying all of TradeBook every night would copy mostly what the lake already has. So the extractor now keeps a watermark: the end of the last good window, stored as a small blob in the landing container. The first command shows there is none yet, and the second sets it to batch forty one's window end, the point the full load covered. The query underneath asks TradeBook about every row's updated at: four hundred and eighteen L Cs now, the newest changed late on the thirty first. Lookup is the extractor's first step, and it copies nothing. It counts the rows whose updated at is after the watermark, and no later than tonight's window end, two o'clock on the first of November. The window is open at the start and closed at the end, so a row stamped exactly on a boundary belongs to one batch, never two. One hundred and twenty of the four hundred and eighteen changed. The side pane draws it as one line of time: the full load, the watermark, tonight's window, and the next watermark, greyed until batch forty two has been delivered and checked. Next, lookup writes down what it found, before anything is copied.

Lookup now leaves something behind: a manifest, a small J SON file in batch forty two's folder. It is written first, before a single row is copied, and that order is the point. The highlighted lines build it from what lookup just learned. The window, with its start and its end. The number of rows the copy must deliver, one hundred and twenty. The files the batch will hold, one C S V. And the table's columns with their PostgreSQL types, read from the database's own catalogue, so a column that disappears or changes type upstream will show up as a difference rather than a surprise. The terminal shows lookup writing it, and the listing beneath shows the landing container: batch forty one's file, and batch forty two's folder, holding only the manifest so far. In the side pane is the blob itself, read back from the lake: the batch, the window, one hundred and twenty expected rows, one file, and ten typed columns, folded in the middle. Above it, the order of the night. Lookup writes the promise. The copy, still to come, writes the data. And the gate called G one will hold the folder to the promise before anything downstream may read it. Next, the copy runs, on a night when the promise is not kept.

This is a night that goes wrong, run once and then thrown away, so the course carries on from the manifest. The new file is g one dot p y, the landing gate. It reads the manifest, lists the batch folder, and checks three things: every promised file is there, the columns are the ones declared, and the rows add up to the expected count. Each check prints what it found against what was promised, and the batch passes only if all three match. The copy reads the manifest's window and writes one hundred and seventeen rows. G one compares: one file of one, ten columns of ten, and one hundred and seventeen rows of one hundred and twenty. Fail. The batch is not published, and the watermark has not moved. The side pane tells the story of the night. At two o'clock, lookup counted one hundred and twenty rows in the window. Seven seconds later, the desk amended three letters of credit, and each one's updated at moved past the window's end, out of tonight's batch. When the copy ran, they were no longer in its window. Nothing crashed, and no error was raised: without the gate, a short batch would have flowed on to Bronze and to the morning's numbers. Next, we make the rerun safe.

A failed night has to be run again, and write once gets in the way: the short file is already in the folder, and a retry would be refused. So the rule changes. A batch folder stays open until it is sealed, and while it is open, a retry overwrites the same path. The copy step first checks for a file called underscore success, and refuses if it exists; otherwise it writes the part file, overwriting. The new commit step runs G one, and only if it passes writes underscore success, and only then moves the watermark. In the terminal, the copy runs twice, as a retry would, and both times writes one hundred and twenty rows to the same file: running it again changes nothing. Commit runs the gate, all three checks pass, the batch is sealed, and the watermark moves to two o'clock on the first of November. One more copy is refused: the batch is sealed. The side pane shows the folder's life, open, committed, sealed, and what it holds now: the manifest from lookup, one part file written twice, and the seal. The order matters. If the machine fails between sealing and moving the watermark, the next run finds a sealed batch, and runs only the commit again. Next, the files that do not come from TradeBook at all.

Two files do not come from TradeBook at all. TradeBook knows legal entities, each company that applies for a letter of credit, but only the risk team knows which entities belong together as one group, and what each group may borrow. Those two facts arrive as files from the risk team, sitting in the project's reference folder. The terminal shows the first lines of the mapping: three Woodgrove companies, all in the Woodgrove group. Reference dot p y publishes both files to their own container, reference, in a folder named for the date they hold for, as of the thirty first of October. They are not deliveries in the landing sense: no watermark, no batch number, and they never pass through Bronze. The listing confirms the two paths. The side pane shows why the zones are separate. On the left, TradeBook's letters of credit go to landing, then Bronze, which keeps every version, then Silver. On the right, the risk team's files go to the reference zone, and Silver reads them directly, after checking them itself in Course nine. Below is the limits file as the lake now holds it: Woodgrove, ten million dollars; Contoso in two currencies, never added together; Fabrikam, three million euros; Northwind, eight million dollars. Next, who is allowed to read a batch.

Last in this course: who may read what lands, and for how long it stays. This frame was recorded on Azure, against the same account. The session first applies one more Terraform resource, a lifecycle policy, then publishes the reference files to the real lake with the same script that ran against the emulator: only the environment changed, a U R L and a sign in instead of a connection string. There are three ways in, and the table in the side pane holds one of each, read from the terminal. R B A C grants a role on the whole account: here, Storage Blob Data Contributor, given to the identity that deployed it. An access control list works per directory, like file permissions: on group limits, the owner can read and write, the group can read, and everyone else gets nothing. The third way is a shared access signature, a link that carries its own permission. Share dot p y signs one with a key that Azure lends to the signed in identity, never an account key, because the account has none. The link reads one file for four hours. With its signature, the request returns two hundred. The same address without the signature returns four hundred and nine: public access is off. At the bottom, the lifecycle: landing's batches stay hot for thirty days while Bronze reads them, cool after that, move to archive after ninety, and are deleted after four hundred. Next, the network around all of this.
